---
title: "Binary outcomes: logistic regression with anova_bin()"
description: >
  A walkthrough of anova_bin() on the Berkeley admissions data: analysis of
  deviance, odds ratios, marginal probabilities, separation, frequency
  weights and robust standard errors.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4, dpi = 96, out.width = "100%")
```

```{r libs}
library(anovakit)
```

`anova_bin()` fits a logistic regression of a two-level outcome (admitted or
not, healed or not) on one or more grouping variables. It reports an analysis
of deviance table, odds ratios, marginal probabilities and pairwise odds
ratios. Use it when each observation is a yes/no outcome, or when you have a
table of such outcomes with a count in each row.

For counts of events, use `anova_count()` ([walkthrough](counts.html)); for
other response distributions, `anova_glm()` ([walkthrough](glm.html)).
[Choose an analysis](choosing.html) sets out the choice.

## The data

`UCBAdmissions` is a three-way table of the 4,526 applications to the six
largest graduate departments at Berkeley in 1973, by outcome, gender and
department. `as.data.frame()` turns it into one row per combination, with the
number of applicants in `Freq`.

```{r data}
ucb <- as.data.frame(UCBAdmissions)
head(ucb)
sum(ucb$Freq)
```

In these data the overall admission rates and the department-level rates point
in different directions:

```{r data-rates}
# Overall admission rate by gender
round(prop.table(xtabs(Freq ~ Gender + Admit, data = ucb), 1), 3)

# Admission rate by department and gender, and where each gender applied
admitted <- xtabs(Freq ~ Dept + Gender, data = ucb[ucb$Admit == "Admitted", ])
applied  <- xtabs(Freq ~ Dept + Gender, data = ucb)
round(admitted / applied, 3)
applied
```

```{r data-inline, include = FALSE}
rate <- prop.table(xtabs(Freq ~ Gender + Admit, data = ucb), 1)
```

Across all departments, `r round(100 * rate["Male", "Admitted"], 1)`% of men
and `r round(100 * rate["Female", "Admitted"], 1)`% of women were admitted.
Within departments the gap mostly disappears, and in department A it reverses.
The last table explains why: most women applied to departments C to F, which
admitted a third or fewer of their applicants, while just over half of the men
applied to A or B, which admitted most of theirs. Department is associated with
both gender and admission, so a comparison of genders that ignores it is
confounded. This is Simpson's paradox, and a model with both variables
separates the two.

Each row of `ucb` stands for `Freq` identical applicants, so the counts go in
as frequency weights. For later comparison, here is the same data with one row
per applicant:

```{r data-expand}
applicants <- ucb[rep(seq_len(nrow(ucb)), ucb$Freq),
                  c("Admit", "Gender", "Dept")]
nrow(applicants)
```

## Fitting the model

### Which outcome is the success

The response can be a factor with two observed levels, a logical, a numeric
0/1 column, or a character column with two values. The function models the
probability of one level, the *success*. By default that is the second level
of the factor, as in `glm()`. For `Admit` the second level is `"Rejected"`:

```{r success-default}
levels(ucb$Admit)
default <- anova_bin(ucb, "Admit", "Gender", weights = "Freq", plots = FALSE)
default$notes[1]
```

Every odds ratio from that model would be an odds ratio of *rejection*. Name
the level you want with `success`. A logical response models `TRUE`, a 0/1
response models `1`, and a character response is sorted in the C locale, so
the default does not depend on your session.

### The fit

Admission modelled on gender and department, additively:

```{r fit}
fit <- anova_bin(ucb, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"), weights = "Freq",
                 success = "Admitted")
fit
```

Reading the printout from the top:

- The method and the call.
- `Observations used: 24`. This counts *rows* of `$data_used`, not
  applicants: each row carries its weight, and the weights add up to
  `r format(sum(fit$data_used$Freq), big.mark = ",")`.
- The omnibus table, with a heading that says what it holds: Type II tests,
  likelihood-ratio chi-square statistics.
- The notes: which level is modelled, how the marginal means are laid out for
  an additive model, and why there is no dispersion statistic. They are
  discussed [below](#what-the-notes-say).
- The plots that were built (they are not drawn until you ask).

`summary(fit)` prints all of this plus the assumption tables, the odds ratios,
the marginal probabilities and the pairwise comparisons. The sections below
take the components one at a time.

## The omnibus test

```{r anova}
fit$anova
```

Each row is a likelihood-ratio test: `statistic` is the increase in deviance
when the term is dropped, referred to a chi-square distribution on `df`
degrees of freedom. Type II means each factor is tested after the other, so
the `Gender` row asks whether gender predicts admission *among applicants to
the same department*. It does not (p = `r signif(fit$anova$p_value[1], 3)`).
Department matters a great deal.

Compare the model with gender alone:

```{r anova-alone}
alone <- anova_bin(ucb, "Admit", "Gender", weights = "Freq",
                   success = "Admitted", plots = FALSE)
alone$anova
```

Without department the gender statistic is
`r round(alone$anova$statistic, 1)` on 1 degree of freedom. Adjusting for
department brings it down to `r round(fit$anova$statistic[1], 2)`.

### The model as a whole

`$model_stats` holds statistics for the whole model:

```{r model-stats}
fit$model_stats
```

`lr_vs_null` is the likelihood-ratio test of this model against one with no
predictors (the null deviance minus the deviance, on
`r fit$model_stats$lr_vs_null$df` degrees of freedom). `mcfadden_r2` is
McFadden's pseudo R squared, `1 - deviance / null deviance`: the model removes
`r round(100 * fit$model_stats$mcfadden_r2, 1)`% of the deviance. It is not a
proportion of variance and runs lower than the R squared of a linear model, so
judge it against other logistic models. `success_level` repeats which level
was modelled, so a saved result says what its odds ratios are odds of. `AIC`,
`BIC` and `logLik` use the prior weights, and are there to compare models
fitted to the same data.

## Effect sizes

`$effect_sizes` holds odds ratios, one per coefficient, each a level against
its factor's reference level:

```{r effect-sizes}
es_cols <- c("factor", "comparison", "odds_ratio", "conf_low", "conf_high",
             "p_value", "ci_method")
print(fit$effect_sizes[, es_cols], digits = 3)
```

`factor` names the grouping variable and `comparison` says what the ratio
compares. The first row is the odds of admission for women divided by the odds
for men, in the same department: `r round(fit$effect_sizes$odds_ratio[1], 3)`,
with an interval that comfortably includes 1. The department rows compare each
department with A; in department F the odds of admission are
`r round(fit$effect_sizes$odds_ratio[6], 3)` times those in A, whatever the
applicant's gender. The columns left out above, `term`, `se_log_or` and
`statistic`, hold the coefficient's name, its standard error on the log-odds
scale and its Wald z statistic.

Put the adjusted odds ratio beside the one from the gender-only model:

```{r effect-simpson}
rbind(alone = alone$effect_sizes[, es_cols],
      adjusted = fit$effect_sizes[1, es_cols])
```

Ignoring department, women's odds of admission were about half of men's;
comparing applicants to the same department, they were slightly higher.

The odds ratios always come from a reference-coded fit of the same model, so
each one is a level against the reference level whatever `type`, the global
`contrasts` option or the class of the factor. `$anova` still comes from the
Type II or Type III fit, which describes the same fitted probabilities.

### Profile or Wald intervals

`ci_method = "profile"` (the default) gives profile-likelihood intervals, which
follow the shape of the likelihood rather than assuming it is quadratic. With
thousands of observations the two kinds agree closely:

```{r ci-wald}
wald <- anova_bin(ucb, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"), weights = "Freq",
                  success = "Admitted", ci_method = "wald", plots = FALSE)
data.frame(comparison = fit$effect_sizes$comparison,
           profile_low = fit$effect_sizes$conf_low,
           profile_high = fit$effect_sizes$conf_high,
           wald_low = wald$effect_sizes$conf_low,
           wald_high = wald$effect_sizes$conf_high)
```

They part company in small samples and, above all, under separation, where
only the profile interval means anything (see [Separation](#separation)).

Profiling refits the model several times for each coefficient. The model
has only grouping factors, so the refits run on the data collapsed to one
weighted row per cell and outcome, which has the same likelihood. The number
of rows therefore does not add to the cost, but the number of coefficients
does. Left at its default, `ci_method` gives Wald intervals instead, with a
note, when the model has more than 50 coefficients. That holds under
separation too, except that an odds ratio separation drives to infinity or to
zero still gets its profile interval, since a Wald interval means nothing
there. `ci_method = "profile"` given explicitly always profiles every
coefficient.

### Choosing the reference level

`reference` takes a named list, one level per factor:

```{r reference}
flipped <- anova_bin(ucb, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"), weights = "Freq",
                     success = "Admitted",
                     reference = list(Gender = "Female", Dept = "F"),
                     plots = FALSE)
print(flipped$effect_sizes[, es_cols], digits = 3)
all.equal(flipped$anova, fit$anova)
```

The ratios are now men against women and each department against F. The
omnibus table is unchanged, because the reference level changes what the
coefficients compare and leaves the fitted model as it was.

## Marginal means and comparisons

`$emmeans` holds estimated marginal probabilities of the success level, with
intervals built on the logit scale and back-transformed, so they stay between
0 and 1:

```{r emmeans}
print(fit$emmeans, digits = 3)
```

Because the model is additive, each factor is reported on its own (the `term`
column says which), averaged over the levels of the other. The averaging gives
each department equal weight on the log-odds scale before transforming back,
so the gender rows are not the raw admission rates of
`r round(rate["Male", "Admitted"], 3)` and
`r round(rate["Female", "Admitted"], 3)`. They are the probabilities for a
hypothetical applicant spread evenly over the six departments, which is the
comparison the adjusted model makes.

`$posthoc` holds the pairwise comparisons, as odds ratios:

```{r posthoc}
ph_cols <- c("term", "contrast", "ratio", "conf_low", "conf_high", "p_value",
             "p_adjusted")
print(fit$posthoc[, ph_cols], digits = 3)
```

Each `ratio` is the odds for the first group in `contrast` divided by the odds
for the second, so the gender row, `Male / Female`, is the reciprocal of the
`Female vs Male` odds ratio in `$effect_sizes`. `p_value` is the unadjusted
p-value and `p_adjusted` the Tukey-adjusted one (the method is in the
`adjustment` column). Each factor is its own family: gender has one comparison,
so its two p-values are equal; department has 15, and the adjustment raises
them. The adjusted p-values printed as 0 are below the precision of the Tukey
calculation (about 1e-10); `summary(fit)` prints them as `< 1e-10`. The
intervals are simultaneous for each family.

`adjust` changes the method: `"tukey"` (the default), `"sidak"`,
`"scheffe"`, `"dunnettx"`, `"bonferroni"`, `"holm"`, `"hochberg"`,
`"hommel"`, `"BH"`, `"BY"`, `"fdr"` or `"none"`. A step-down method such as
Holm adjusts p-values but cannot be turned into intervals, and `$notes` says
what the intervals use instead:

```{r adjust-holm}
holm <- anova_bin(ucb, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"), weights = "Freq",
                  success = "Admitted", adjust = "holm", plots = FALSE)
grep("adjustment", holm$notes, value = TRUE)
```

The department intervals are Bonferroni intervals, while the p-values are
Holm's. The gender family has a single comparison, which needs no adjustment of
either kind, so there is no note about it.

## Checking assumptions

From grouped data like these, a logistic regression has few distributional
assumptions to check: the outcome is binary, the observations are independent,
and the log-odds are additive in the factors (the `interaction` option
[below](#interaction-and-type) tests that). `$assumptions` has two elements.

```{r assumptions-dispersion}
fit$assumptions$dispersion
```

`dispersion` is always `NA`, and a note says why. For a 0/1 response the
Pearson dispersion carries no information about overdispersion: in a model
saturated in the cells it equals N / (N - k) whatever the data, and it changes
when the same trials are grouped into weighted rows. Computing it on the two
versions of this data set, which describe the same fit, shows the second
point:

```{r assumptions-pearson}
pearson <- function(m) sum(residuals(m, type = "pearson")^2) / df.residual(m)
one_row <- anova_bin(applicants, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"),
                     success = "Admitted", plots = FALSE)
c(weighted_table = pearson(fit$model),
  one_row_per_applicant = pearson(one_row$model))
```

`proportions` is the observed share of each response level in each cell. With
weights, `n` and `group_total` are weighted counts, and `rows` and
`group_rows` give the number of data rows behind them:

```{r assumptions-proportions}
props <- fit$assumptions$proportions
props[props$Admit == "Admitted", ]
```

Look at this table before trusting the model. It shows the raw material and
the cells with few observations: department B had only
`r props$group_total[props$.cell == "Female : B" & props$Admit == "Admitted"]`
women applicants. When fewer than about 5 events or non-events are expected in
a cell, `$notes` warns that the likelihood-ratio test is liberal. No cell here
comes close; the separation example below shows the note.

The [diagnostics article](diagnostics.html) covers the checks across the
package.

### Separation

When every observation in a group has the same outcome, the maximum-likelihood
odds ratio for that group is infinite. `glm()` still reports convergence, with
an enormous coefficient and an even larger standard error. Here is a small
constructed table in which every patient in the `high` arm healed:

```{r separation}
healing <- data.frame(
  arm    = factor(rep(c("control", "low", "high"), each = 2),
                  levels = c("control", "low", "high")),
  healed = rep(c("no", "yes"), times = 3),
  n      = c(9, 6, 5, 10, 0, 15)
)
healing
sep_fit <- anova_bin(healing, "healed", "arm", weights = "n")
sep_fit
```

Besides the success level and the dispersion, the notes record four things.
The row with a count of zero was dropped: a
zero-weight row contributes nothing, and it is counted in `$n_removed`, which
is why the printout says 5 observations were used. Separation was detected in
`arm = high`. The profile interval for that odds ratio is open on one side.
The data are also sparse: with 15 patients an arm, fewer than 5 non-events are
expected in each arm if the arms do not differ, so the likelihood-ratio test in
the table is liberal. The note names two tests that hold their level better,
and both are one line of code:

```{r separation-exact}
anova(sep_fit$model, test = "Rao")
fisher.test(xtabs(n ~ arm + healed, data = healing))
```

Both p-values are larger than the likelihood-ratio test's
`r format(signif(sep_fit$anova$p_value, 2), scientific = FALSE)`, though the
conclusion stands.

```{r separation-es}
print(sep_fit$effect_sizes[, es_cols], digits = 3)
sep_wald <- anova_bin(healing, "healed", "arm", weights = "n",
                      ci_method = "wald", plots = FALSE)
print(sep_wald$effect_sizes[, es_cols], digits = 3)
```

The point estimate for `high vs control` is meaningless, and so is its Wald
p-value of `r round(sep_fit$effect_sizes$p_value[2], 2)`. The profile interval
still carries information: it runs from
`r round(sep_fit$effect_sizes$conf_low[2], 1)` to infinity, so the data rule
out an odds ratio below about `r round(sep_fit$effect_sizes$conf_low[2])`. The
Wald interval, from 0 to infinity, rules out nothing. That difference is the
reason `ci_method = "profile"` is the default.

The separation note also warns that the separated arm's marginal probability
and the comparisons involving it are affected. They are Wald-based, and as
uninformative as the Wald odds ratio:

```{r separation-emm}
print(sep_fit$emmeans, digits = 3)
print(sep_fit$posthoc[, c("contrast", "ratio", "conf_low", "conf_high",
                          "p_adjusted")], digits = 3)
```

For a real analysis, follow the note: a penalised fit such as
`logistf::logistf()`, or collapsing the level with another, gives finite
estimates.

## Plots

`fit$plots` holds two ggplot2 objects. Neither is drawn until you ask for
it, with `plot(fit, "name")` or `fit$plots$name`.

```{r plot-proportions}
plot(fit, "proportions")
```

The `proportions` plot stacks the observed share of each outcome in each cell
(gender by department here), labelled with percentages. Look for cells whose
proportions differ from their neighbours, cells near 0% or 100% (the warning
sign of separation), and whether a pattern in one factor holds across the
levels of the other. Here the within-department gender differences are small
next to the differences between departments, and department A is the one
where women did clearly better.

```{r plot-emmeans}
plot(fit, "emmeans")
```

The `emmeans` plot shows the estimated marginal probabilities with their
intervals, one panel per factor because the model is additive. Intervals that
do not overlap are clearly different; for overlapping ones, read the
comparisons in `$posthoc`. Each plot is a ggplot, so it can be modified with
`+`:

```{r plot-custom}
plot(fit, "emmeans") +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  ggplot2::labs(y = "Probability of admission")
```

[Plots and themes](visuals.html) covers customisation.

## Options

### `interaction` and `type`

The model above is additive: it assumes the gender odds ratio is the same in
every department. `interaction = TRUE` fits the full factorial and tests that
assumption. The first grouping variable goes on the x axis of the `emmeans`
plot, so department comes first here:

```{r interaction}
fit_int <- anova_bin(ucb, "Admit", c("Dept", "Gender"), weights = "Freq",
                     success = "Admitted", interaction = TRUE)
fit_int$anova
```

The `Dept:Gender` row is a likelihood-ratio test of whether the gender odds
ratio differs between departments (p =
`r signif(fit_int$anova$p_value[3], 2)`). With an interaction, each lower-order
odds ratio is taken at the reference level of the factors it interacts with,
and the interaction rows are ratios of odds ratios; the `comparison` column
says which:

```{r interaction-es}
print(fit_int$effect_sizes[, es_cols], digits = 3)
```

The `Gender` row is the gender odds ratio in department A, and each
`Dept:Gender` row is the gender odds ratio in another department divided by
the one in A. All of them are below 1, so department A is the odd one out.

`$emmeans` now has one row per cell, and `$posthoc` compares every pair of
cells (`r nrow(fit_int$posthoc)` comparisons, most of them of no interest).
For women against men within each department, pass `$emmeans_object` to
emmeans directly:

```{r interaction-contrast}
emmeans::contrast(fit_int$emmeans_object, method = "revpairwise", by = "Dept")
```

The grid carries emmeans' own default confidence level rather than
`conf_level`, so give `level =` when you summarise it.

```{r interaction-plot}
plot(fit_int, "emmeans")
```

With department on the x axis and one line per gender, the two lines lie
almost on top of each other everywhere except in department A.

With an interaction in the model, `type` matters. Type II tests each main
effect assuming the interaction is absent; Type III (fitted under sum-to-zero
contrasts) tests it averaged over the other factor's levels:

```{r interaction-type3}
fit_int3 <- anova_bin(ucb, "Admit", c("Dept", "Gender"), weights = "Freq",
                      success = "Admitted", interaction = TRUE, type = "III",
                      plots = FALSE)
fit_int3$anova
all.equal(fit_int3$effect_sizes, fit_int$effect_sizes)
```

Only the omnibus table changes: the odds ratios come from a reference-coded
fit whatever `type` is. With an interaction this clear, neither main-effect row
tells the whole story; report the interaction and the within-department odds
ratios.

### `test_statistic`

The omnibus table uses likelihood-ratio tests by default.
`test_statistic = "Wald"` gives Wald chi-square tests instead:

```{r wald-test}
anova_bin(ucb, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"), weights = "Freq",
          success = "Admitted", test_statistic = "Wald", plots = FALSE)$anova
```

The two agree closely for gender and differ for department, whose effects are
large. The likelihood-ratio test is the better default. The Wald test is there
mainly because it can use a robust covariance (next section).

### Weights and `vcov_type`

`weights` names a column of prior weights. Whole-number weights, some above 1,
are frequency weights: a row with weight `w` counts as `w` identical
observations, so the 24-row table `ucb` gives the same results as
`applicants`, with one row per applicant. `vcov_type` asks for
heteroskedasticity-consistent (sandwich) standard errors, `"HC0"` to `"HC4"`,
which need the sandwich package. With frequency weights they too are
computed as they would be on the expanded data. `one_row` was fitted on
`applicants` [above](#checking-assumptions):

```{r weights-hc3}
hc_table <- anova_bin(ucb, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"), weights = "Freq",
                      success = "Admitted", vcov_type = "HC3", plots = FALSE)
hc_rows <- anova_bin(applicants, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"),
                     success = "Admitted", vcov_type = "HC3", plots = FALSE)
all.equal(fit$anova, one_row$anova)
c(table = fit$model_stats$BIC, applicants = one_row$model_stats$BIC)
data.frame(comparison = fit$effect_sizes$comparison,
           se_table = fit$effect_sizes$se_log_or,
           se_applicants = one_row$effect_sizes$se_log_or,
           hc3_table = hc_table$effect_sizes$se_log_or,
           hc3_applicants = hc_rows$effect_sizes$se_log_or)
```

```{r weights-naive, include = FALSE}
naive <- sqrt(diag(sandwich::vcovHC(fit$model, type = "HC3")))[-1]
naive_ratio <- unname(naive / hc_table$effect_sizes$se_log_or)
```

The model-based standard errors agree to five or more significant figures (the
rest is `glm()`'s convergence tolerance), and BIC is the same because its
penalty uses the `r format(sum(ucb$Freq), big.mark = ",")` observations the
weights represent, not the 24 rows. The HC3 standard errors from the table
and from one row per applicant are the same, and close to the model-based
ones. `sandwich::vcovHC()` applied to the weighted table directly would treat
each row as one unit, and here gives standard errors
`r floor(min(naive_ratio))` to `r ceiling(max(naive_ratio))` times too large.

The notes record what the robust covariance was used for:

```{r weights-hc3-notes}
grep("robust", hc_table$notes, value = TRUE, ignore.case = TRUE)
```

Robust standard errors reach the odds ratios, the marginal means and the
comparisons. The likelihood-ratio omnibus test compares deviances and does
not use them; set `test_statistic = "Wald"` for an omnibus test that does. The
odds-ratio intervals become Wald intervals, since a profile likelihood cannot
use a sandwich covariance.

Weights that are not whole numbers are not frequencies. They are used as
given, as `glm()` uses prior weights, so their scale matters, and `$notes`
says so. `AIC`, `BIC` and `logLik` in `$model_stats` are then `NA`, with a
note, because R's binomial log-likelihood rounds the weights; McFadden's R
squared and `lr_vs_null` come from the deviances and are still reported.
Unequal weights of this kind also inflate the likelihood-ratio statistics. A
further note estimates by how much and recommends `vcov_type = "HC3"`. Two
more notes pass on the "non-integer #successes" warnings from `glm()` and
`car::Anova()`.
[Weights and robust standard errors](weights.html) sets out the rules for
every kind of weight and for `vcov_type` across the package.

### `conf_level` and `posthoc`

`conf_level` sets the level of every interval in the result: odds ratios,
marginal probabilities and comparisons. `posthoc = FALSE` skips the pairwise
comparisons, which saves time when there are many cells; `$notes` records how
many were skipped, and `$effect_sizes` is still computed.

```{r conf-level}
narrow <- anova_bin(ucb, "Admit", c("Gender", "Dept"), weights = "Freq",
                    success = "Admitted", conf_level = 0.90, posthoc = FALSE,
                    plots = FALSE)
narrow$effect_sizes[1, c("comparison", "odds_ratio", "conf_low", "conf_high")]
narrow$emmeans[1:2, c("Gender", "estimate", "conf_low", "conf_high")]
grep("posthoc|still reports", narrow$notes, value = TRUE)
```

## What the notes say

```{r notes}
fit$notes
```

- The first note names the level being modelled. Check it on every fit: an
  odds ratio of admission and an odds ratio of rejection are reciprocals, and
  confusing them reverses every conclusion.
- The second says that, in an additive model, the marginal means and
  comparisons are reported for each factor separately, averaged over the
  other, with each factor's comparisons adjusted as a separate family.
- The third explains why `$assumptions$dispersion` is `NA`.

Other fits in this article showed the notes you may meet elsewhere: a
zero-weight row dropped, separation detected and an open-ended profile
interval, sparse data, a step-down adjustment, and robust standard errors with
frequency weights. [Working with results](results.html) explains how
`$notes` fits with the rest of the object.

## Reporting the result

```{r report-inline, include = FALSE}
a <- fit$anova
es <- fit$effect_sizes
fmt_p <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "< 0.001" else paste("=", signif(p, 2))
```

A write-up of the adjusted analysis might read:

> Admission was modelled by logistic regression on gender and department for
> the `r format(sum(ucb$Freq), big.mark = ",")` applicants. Department was
> strongly associated with admission (likelihood-ratio
> χ²(`r a$df[2]`) = `r round(a$statistic[2], 1)`, p `r fmt_p(a$p_value[2])`),
> but gender was not once department was taken into account
> (χ²(`r a$df[1]`) = `r round(a$statistic[1], 2)`, p `r fmt_p(a$p_value[1])`;
> odds ratio for women against men `r sprintf("%.2f", es$odds_ratio[1])`, 95%
> profile-likelihood CI `r sprintf("%.2f", es$conf_low[1])` to
> `r sprintf("%.2f", es$conf_high[1])`). The unadjusted odds ratio of
> `r sprintf("%.2f", alone$effect_sizes$odds_ratio)` is accounted for by
> the departments women applied to. The gender odds ratio varied between
> departments (χ²(`r fit_int$anova$df[3]`) =
> `r round(fit_int$anova$statistic[3], 1)`, p
> `r fmt_p(fit_int$anova$p_value[3])`) and was largest in department A.
